Gittaim
GIT-ay-im
proper noun
Hebrew Gittayim, “two winepresses”; a town of Benjamin to which the men of Beeroth fled and sojourned; reinhabited after the exile.

📖 Biblical Definition

Gittaim, “two winepresses,” was a town associated with Benjamin, remembered as the refuge of the Beerothites: “And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day” (2Sa 4:3). Beeroth was one of the cities of the Gibeonites, reckoned to Benjamin, and for some cause its people fled and became sojourners — resident strangers — in Gittaim. After the Babylonian exile the town was inhabited again, for the children of Benjamin dwelt at Gittaim among other places (Neh 11:33). The name, “two winepresses,” speaks of a place of vintage, where the grapes were trodden and the wine ran out. Yet its history is a history of displacement: a people driven from their home, dwelling as strangers in another’s town for generations. Gittaim preaches the pilgrim condition of the people of God, who are strangers and sojourners on the earth, confessing that here they have no continuing city but seek one to come. As the Beerothites sojourned in Gittaim, so the saints sojourn in this world, treading through the winepress of affliction toward the city whose builder and maker is God, where the tears of exile are wiped away for ever.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Benjamin, “two winepresses,” refuge of the displaced Beerothites (2Sa 4:3; Neh 11:33); a witness to the pilgrim condition of God’s people, strangers and sojourners on the earth.

📖 Key Scripture

2Sa 4:3 — "And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day.)"

Deu 33:12 — "And of Benjamin he said, The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him; and the LORD shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders."

Josh 18:11 — "And the lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families: and the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph."

Josh 18:20 — "And Jordan was the border of it on the east side. This was the inheritance of the children of Benjamin, by the coasts thereof round about, according to their families."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A town of Benjamin sheltering displaced sojourners; it recovers the pilgrim condition of God’s people, strangers on the earth seeking a city to come.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A refuge-town raises no modern quarrel. Its story is one of displacement: the Beerothites fled there and dwelt as strangers for generations, a picture of the pilgrim life.

The principle to recover is that the people of God are sojourners on the earth. As the Beerothites dwelt as strangers in Gittaim, so the saints confess themselves pilgrims here, having no continuing city but seeking one to come. Treading through the winepress of affliction, they look for the city whose builder and maker is God, where the long exile ends and every tear is wiped away.
